city.zayton.market.desc: The quay of Zayton runs the length of the water and is never quiet. Pepper comes ashore in sacks the height of a man; there are pearls weighed out in little brass scales, and lignaloes and sandalwood stacked like cordwood. You must know that the merchant pays dearly here: the Kaan takes a tamghā on everything, ten in the hundred, and the ship's charge on top of it — thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper. Between the freight and the Kaan's due a man pays out a good half of what his cargo is worth. And yet on the other half he makes so great a profit that he is always glad to come back with more.
city.zayton.market.name: The Quay at Zayton
city.zayton.name: Zayton
city.zayton.shrine.desc: Above the anchorage, on a hill that catches the first light off the sea, stands the temple of the sea-goddess. Her gilded image faces south over the water; at her feet lie the offerings of shipmasters — paper burnt, rice set out, a cup of wine. No master of this coast puts out without going up to her first, and none of them calls it fortune-telling. They call it asking.
city.zayton.shrine.name: The Temple of the Sea
city.zayton.wonder: You have heard men speak of Alexandria and her hundred spired warehouses. Know this: for every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred such come in to this haven of Zayton — aye, and more too. The ships of India crowd the water so thickly that their masts, seen from the hill at sunrise, look like a burnt forest. And it is not only pepper. Precious stones, pearls, spicery of every kind that grows, silk enough to clothe an empire — all of it passes through this quay, and the Kaan's clerks are not finished counting before the next season's fleet appears on the horizon.
codex.cx-fanfang.body: A street of the port given over to the merchants of India, Persia and the Arab lands, with their own houses of prayer standing within hearing of the sea-goddess's gongs.
codex.cx-fanfang.name: The Foreign Quarter
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.body: For every shipload of pepper that reaches Alexandria bound for Christendom, a hundred come in to Zayton. It is one of the two greatest havens in the world for commerce.
codex.cx-hundred-shiploads.name: A Hundred Shiploads
codex.cx-lots.body: The cylinder is shaken until a single numbered slip falls out. The number is read against a book of verses. The verse does not answer the question asked; it names the thing the asker had not weighed.
codex.cx-lots.name: Reading the Slips
codex.cx-monsoon.body: The wind of the Indian sea turns with the seasons. Ships out of Zayton for the Indies wait upon it, and a master who sails against it does not come back to say so.
codex.cx-monsoon.name: The Monsoon
codex.cx-pepper-freight.body: Thirty in the hundred on small wares, forty on lignaloes and sandalwood and other bulky goods, and four and forty on pepper.
codex.cx-pepper-freight.name: Freight Rates at Zayton
codex.cx-sea-goddess.body: A goddess of this coast to whom shipmasters go before sailing. Her temple keeps a cylinder of numbered slips; a slip is drawn and read against a book of verses.
codex.cx-sea-goddess.name: The Goddess of the Sea
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.body: Ten in the hundred on all merchandise landed at Zayton, including precious stones and pearls — the Great Kaan takes the tamghā on everything. With the ship's freight added, a merchant pays out half his cargo's worth before he has sold a grain of it.
codex.cx-zayton-tithe.name: The Kaan's Tamghā

div.bazi.apprentice: The astrologer studies your birth date with narrowed eyes, drawing a chart of eight characters in black ink. 'Your wood is strong but your fire is weak,' she says. 'This is not a judgment. It is a compass. The roads that suit a fire person will burn you out. The roads that suit a wood person will let you grow. I will teach you to read your own chart — but first you must accept that you cannot walk every road.'
div.bazi.desc: The Four Pillars of Destiny examine the hour, day, month, and year of your birth against the elemental cycles of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. The chart reveals what kind of traveller you are — which regions suit your nature, which companions strengthen you, and which years bring opportunity. Cost: 400 coins. Horizon: three years.

div.iching.apprentice: The old scholar unrolls a strip of yellow silk covered with broken and unbroken lines. 'These are not fortunes,' he says. 'They are maps. Each hexagram is a landscape — mountains, rivers, thunder, wind. You do not ask if you will succeed. You ask: which road through this landscape is mine?' He places three coins in your open palm. 'Cast them. We will read what the earth writes.'
div.iching.desc: The Book of Changes reveals the shape of the road ahead. Ask not whether fortune favours you, but which direction aligns with the moment. Cast three coins six times to form a hexagram; each line speaks of movement or stillness. The reading shows which routes open and which close. Cost: 200 coins. Horizon: one season.

div.lot.apprentice: The temple keeper shakes the bamboo cylinder until a single numbered stick clatters onto the stone floor. He picks it up, squints at the number, and turns to a cabinet of a hundred drawers. 'Each lot is a verse,' he says, selecting a slip of paper. 'Each verse is a warning or a permission. The gods do not prophesy — they advise. Learn to hear the difference, and you will never be lost.'
div.lot.desc: Temple lots give a direct answer to a single question — yes or no, with a warning. Shake the bamboo cylinder until one numbered stick falls. The keeper reads the corresponding verse from the book. Best for immediate decisions: Should I take this road today? Is this merchant honest? Cost: 50 coins. Horizon: one day.

ending.returned-to-venice.body: After {years} years on the road, you have returned to the city where you began. The Piazza San Marco is smaller than you remembered. The merchants who once seemed rich are now modest traders with modest horizons. Your cargo — {goods} — makes you the wealthiest man in Venice, but wealth no longer interests you. In the evenings, you stand on the Rialto and watch the ships you will never board, their holds full of pepper you no longer need to buy, bound for ports you have already seen. The Doge invites you to dinner; you tell the story of the {cities} cities you have passed through, and no one believes half of it. {faith} has taught you that the journey was the destination. The book you write will be called a fantasy. You will let them believe that.
ending.returned-to-venice.name: The Return
ending.stayed-in-the-east.body: You never went back. Somewhere on the {longestRoute} — the longest road you ever rode — you realised that the traveller you had become no longer belonged in the place that made you. You settled in {cities}, a city of {faith} prayers and merchants who speak {languages} languages. You took a local name. You married. Your children speak a tongue you learned as an adult. At night, when the traders arrive from the west, you listen to news of your birthplace the way you once listened to tales of Cathay — as a story about a country you have visited but no longer live in. In your old age, a young traveller arrives from Venice, full of questions. You answer none of them. Instead, you pour him tea and tell him about the road ahead.
ending.stayed-in-the-east.name: The East
ending.template: After {years} years of travel, you have seen {cities} cities. You crossed {deserts} deserts and sailed {seas} seas. The {longestRoute} taught you the most. {faith} sustained you when nothing else would. This is the story of how you became {final_title} — a name the road gave you, and the road will remember.
ending.witness-of-the-world.body: You have seen {cities} cities, crossed {deserts} deserts, and sailed {seas} seas. Your maps are the most accurate in the world, though only you can read them. Your journals fill a chest — prices, routes, customs, warnings, drawings of plants no physician has described, star-charts no astrologer has drawn. You are not the richest man in the world, nor the most powerful, but you are its greatest witness. When the scholars of {faith} come to interview you in your last years, you dictate for hours, days, weeks, until your voice gives out. They write it all down. The book they produce will be read for a hundred years, and every traveller who follows will follow your footsteps — whether they know your name or not. This is the only immortality that means anything: the road remembers.
ending.witness-of-the-world.name: The Witness
ev.accon.entry.body: Acre — the last bastion of the Crusader kingdom, a fortified port where Latin, Greek, and Arabic merchants trade under the watch of the Templars' tower. Pilgrims embark here for Jerusalem; Venetian galleys unload woolens and load spices for the return voyage.
ev.accon.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.accon.entry.title: Arriving at Accon
ev.aden.entry.body: You must know that in the province of ADEN there is a Prince who is called the Soldan. The people are all Saracens and adorers of Mahommet, and have a great hatred of Christians. There are many towns and villages in the country. This Aden is the port to which many of the ships of India come with their cargoes; and from this haven the merchants carry the goods a distance of seven days further in small vessels. At the end of those seven days they land the goods and load them on camels, and so carry them a land journey of 30 days. This brings them to the river of ALEXANDRIA, and by it they descend to the latter city. It is by this way through Aden that the Saracens of Alexandria receive all their stores of pepper and other spicery; and there is no other route equally good and convenient by which these goods could reach that place.
ev.aden.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.aden.entry.title: Concerning the Province of Aden
ev.alexandria.entry.body: Alexandria, the ancient port of the Pharaohs, now a Mamluk customs gate. The lighthouse that once guided ships from every sea is a ruin, its stones quarried for the city walls. But the harbors still teem with vessels: Indian pepper, Syrian glass, Egyptian grain, and Frankish woolens change hands on the quays. The Venetian and Genoese fondacos compete for warehouse space; the Mamluk customs officers weigh every bale and take their fifth.
ev.alexandria.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.alexandria.entry.title: Arriving at Alexandria
ev.antiochia.entry.body: Antioch — once the third city of Rome, now a frontier town of the Mamluk sultanate. Its walls still stand, scarred by a century of crusades and counter-sieges. Silk from Aleppo and wool from Anatolia change hands in its covered bazaar.
ev.antiochia.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.antiochia.entry.title: Arriving at Antiochia
ev.axuma.entry.body: Axum — an ancient Christian kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands, now a shadow of its former glory. The obelisks still stand, and the Church still prays in Ge'ez, but the Red Sea trade has shifted to Aden.
ev.axuma.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.axuma.entry.title: Arriving at Axuma
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.body: Cairo, which the Latins call Babylonia — the greatest city of the Mamluk realm. A hundred minarets rise above the Nile; the citadel of Salah al-Din crowns the hill. The spice markets of the Khan al-Khalili never sleep; merchants from India, Yemen, and the Maghreb crowd the streets. The Caliph's ancient palace is gone, but the Sultan's Mamluk cavalry — ten thousand Circassian and Turkic slave-soldiers — patrol the walls. All goods that pass from the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean must pass through the Babylonia customs, and the Sultan takes a handsome share.
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.babylonia-cairus.entry.title: Arriving at Babylonia Cairus
ev.badashan.entry.body: Badashan is a Province inhabited by people who worship Mahommet, and have a peculiar language. It forms a very great kingdom, and the royalty is hereditary. All those of the royal blood are descended from King Alexander and the daughter of King Darius, who was Lord of the vast Empire of Persia. And all these kings call themselves in the Saracen tongue ZULCARNIAIN, which is as much as to say _Alexander_; and this out of regard for Alexander the Great. It is in this province that those fine and valuable gems the Balas Rubies are found. They are got in certain rocks among the mountains, and in the search for them the people dig great caves underground, just as is done by miners for silver. There is but one special mountain that produces them, and it is called SYGHINAN. The stones are dug on the king’s account, and no one else dares dig in that mountain on pain of forfeiture of life as well as goods; nor may any one carry the stones out of the kingdom.
ev.badashan.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.badashan.entry.title: Of the Province of Badashan
ev.balc.a.body: Balc was once the mother of cities — the capital of Bactria, where Alexander the Great took Roxana of Sogdiana as his bride. Its walls enclosed more ground than any city in Asia, and its temples held treasure from India, Persia, and Greece. Now its broken ramparts, collapsed domes, and empty palaces tell the same story as every city east of the Oxus: the Mongol rider came, and nothing was left standing. Yet the caravans still stop here, and the city is slowly rebuilding from the rubble. The new houses are smaller, built from the stones of the old, but the market is alive again. The King of Balc pays tribute to the Great Kaan, and the trade of lapis lazuli, rubies, and Turkoman horses keeps the city's heart beating.
ev.balc.a.choice.explore: Search the ruins where Alexander married Roxana
ev.balc.a.choice.fragment: Pick up a carved stone from the old city
ev.balc.a.choice.listen: Ask an old man what this city was in its height
ev.balc.a.title: The Ruins of Bactra
ev.balc.b.body: The caravanserai of Balc is one of the largest on the Silk Road — a fortress-sized courtyard ringed with stables for a thousand camels, storerooms stacked with bales of silk and leather sacks of lapis, and chambers for merchants of every nation. Lapis lazuli from the mines of Badakhshan, which lies twelve days east, is the city's chief treasure; it is sold in rough blocks and traded for silver, silk, and spices. Balas rubies from the mountains fetch prices that would buy a ship in Venice. Horses from the Turkoman plains are auctioned in the inner courtyard. The caravanserai never sleeps; fires burn in the arcades all night, and the smell of lamb kebab and saffron rice hangs in the air.
ev.balc.b.choice.lapis: Buy a block of raw lapis lazuli from Badakhshan
ev.balc.b.choice.ruby: Buy a balas ruby — worth a ship in Venice
ev.balc.b.choice.talk_traders: Ask the caravan masters where the roads go
ev.balc.b.title: The Caravanserai of Balc
ev.balc.c.body: On a hill outside the city, a fire-temple of the ancient Persian faith still burns — the Magi tend a flame they say has never been extinguished since the days of Zoroaster, a thousand years before the Prophet. The people call it the Tomb of the Magi, and they say that the three wise men who visited the infant Christ are buried here, in three stone sarcophagi that still bear traces of gold leaf. Pilgrims from Persia, India, and even distant Cathay climb the hill to leave offerings of incense and silver coins. The Magi in their white robes chant the ancient hymns at dawn and dusk. They say that a man who sleeps at the shrine will dream of his own death — and that every dream they have recorded has come true.
ev.balc.c.choice.chant: Listen to the Magi chant at dawn
ev.balc.c.choice.offering: Leave incense at the fire that has never gone out
ev.balc.c.choice.sleep: Sleep at the Tomb of the Magi and wait for a dream
ev.balc.c.title: The Shrine of the Magi
ev.balc.entry.body: Balc is a noble city and a great, though it was much greater in former days. But the Tartars and other nations have greatly ravaged and destroyed it. There were formerly many fine palaces and buildings of marble, and the ruins of them still remain. The people of the city tell that it was here that Alexander took to wife the daughter of Darius. Here, you should be told, is the end of the empire of the Tartar Lord of the Levant. And this city is also the limit of Persia in the direction between east and north-east. Now, let us quit this city, and I will tell you of another country called DOGANA. When you have quitted the city of which I have been speaking, you ride some 12 days between north-east and east, without finding any human habitation, for the people have all taken refuge in fastnesses among the mountains, on account of the Banditti and armies that harassed them. There is plenty of water on the road, and abundance of game; there are lions too. You can get no provisions on the road, and must carry with you all that you require for these 12 days.
ev.balc.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the bājgāh (toll-house)
ev.balc.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.balc.entry.title: Of the City of Balc
ev.baldacum.a.body: The great palace of the Caliph of Baghdad covered more ground than any building in Islam. Its golden dome could be seen three days' journey away across the flat plain of the Tigris. Within were halls hung with silk embroidered with gold thread, gardens watered by channels drawn from the river, courtyards paved with marble brought from every corner of the Caliphate, and the treasury that held the tribute of a hundred nations. The Caliph himself was never seen except by a handful of servants and his vizier. His harem contained a thousand women; his guard was an army of twenty thousand Turkic slaves. And yet when Hulagu came to the walls, all that gold and all those swords could not save him.
ev.baldacum.a.choice.explore: Explore the ruined halls of the Caliph
ev.baldacum.a.choice.listen: Hire a guard to tell you what this place once was
ev.baldacum.a.choice.treasure: Bribe the old warden and search the treasury rubble
ev.baldacum.a.title: The Caliph's Palace
ev.baldacum.b.body: Merchants from India, Persia, Syria, and the Levant crowd the covered markets of Baudas. The bazaars are organized by trade — the silversmiths in one vaulted lane, the silk-merchants in another, the spice-sellers in a third — and each guild maintains its own mosque, bathhouse, and coffee-house. Silk and cloth of gold from Mosul, spices from Hormuz and India, pearls from the Gulf, paper from Samarcand, and Damascus steel blades change hands by the hour. The money-changers sit cross-legged behind low tables covered with mountains of silver dirhams; the merchants drink sherbet cooled with snow brought down from the Kurdish mountains and argue over fractions of a grain of gold.
ev.baldacum.b.choice.brocade: Buy a length of Baghdad brocade worked with gold
ev.baldacum.b.choice.sherbet: Drink sherbet with the money-changers and listen
ev.baldacum.b.choice.spices: Ask the spice-sellers where their wares come from
ev.baldacum.b.title: The Bazaars of Baudas
ev.baldacum.c.body: The story of how Hulagu took this city is still told in the bazaars. The Caliph, trusting in his gold and his twenty thousand guards, refused to pay tribute to the Great Khan and defied the Mongol envoy. Hulagu marched on the city with a host that blackened the plain from horizon to horizon. He broke the dikes of the Tigris and flooded the Mongol camp, but his engineers diverted the water and drained the Caliph's moat. When the walls fell, Hulagu shut the Caliph in his own treasury — a tower full of gold, silver, jewels, and silk — and told him to eat his treasure. The Caliph starved among his wealth, and the city burned for a month.
ev.baldacum.c.choice.listen: Hear the full tale of how Hulagu took the city
ev.baldacum.c.choice.record: Write down the story while it is still told
ev.baldacum.c.choice.search: Search for a coin from before the sack
ev.baldacum.c.title: The Fall of the City
ev.baldacum.entry.body: Baudas is a great city, which used to be the seat of the Calif of all the Saracens in the world, just as Rome is the seat of the Pope of all the Christians. A very great river flows through the city, and by this you can descend to the Sea of India. There is a great traffic of merchants with their goods this way; they descend some eighteen days from Baudas, and then come to a certain city called KISI, where they enter the Sea of India. There is also on the river, as you go from Baudas to Kisi, a great city called BASTRA, surrounded by woods, in which grow the best dates in the world. In Baudas they weave many different kinds of silk stuffs and gold brocades, such as _nasich_, and _nac_, and _cramoisy_, and many another beautiful tissue richly wrought with figures of beasts and birds. It is the noblest and greatest city in all those regions. Now it came to pass on a day in the year of Christ 1255, that the Lord of the Tartars of the Levant, whose name was Alaü, brother to the Great Kaan now reigning, gathered a mighty host and came up against Baudas and took it by storm. It was a great enterprise! for in Baudas there were more than 100,000 horse, besides foot soldiers. And when Alaü had taken the place he found therein a tower of the Califs, which was full of gold and silver and other treasure; in fact the greatest accumulation of treasure in one spot that ever was known. When he beheld that great heap of treasure he was astonished, and, summoning the Calif to his presence, he said to him: “Calif, tell me now why thou hast gathered such a huge treasure? What didst thou mean to do therewith? Knewest thou not that I was thine enemy, and that I was coming against thee with so great an host to cast thee forth of thine heritage? Wherefore didst thou not take of thy gear and employ it in paying knights and soldiers to defend thee and thy city?” The Calif wist not what to answer, and said never a word.
ev.baldacum.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the tamghā-khāna (tax-house)
ev.baldacum.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.baldacum.entry.title: Of the Great City of Baudas, and How It Was Taken
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.body: A calendar master will teach four pillars to read three-year travel windows.
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.choice.ask: Ask how calendars serve the road
ev.baldacum.mentor_bazi.title: Pillars at Baghdad
ev.basora.entry.body: Basra — where the Tigris and Euphrates meet before emptying into the Persian Gulf. A city of canals and palm groves, famous for its dates — the best in the world, according to the merchants who ship them to India. Pearl divers work the oyster beds offshore; the finest gems go to the Caliph's treasury, the rest to the bazaar. Ships bound for Hormuz, India, and Zanzibar load cargo here when the monsoon blows.
ev.basora.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.basora.entry.title: Arriving at Basora
ev.berrhoea.entry.body: Aleppo, known to the Franks as Berrhoea — the caravanserai city of northern Syria. Its covered bazaar stretches for a mile, lined with soap-makers, silk-weavers, and spice merchants. Caravans from Baghdad, Damascus, and Anatolia converge here; the khans are never empty. The citadel on its high mound commands the plain. The governor collects a toll on every camel-load, and the city prospers whether under Mamluk or Mongol rule.
ev.berrhoea.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.berrhoea.entry.title: Arriving at Berrhoea
ev.bethleem.entry.body: Bethlehem — a small town on a hill, holy to Christians as the birthplace of the Lord. Pilgrims come to see the Grotto of the Nativity; the road from Jerusalem is short but steep, and the monasteries offer bread and shelter.
ev.bethleem.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.bethleem.entry.title: Arriving at Bethleem
ev.bochara.entry.body: Bokhara — the dome of Islam in Central Asia, where the madrasas teach law and theology to students from every corner of the Khan's lands. Carpets, silk, and the finest paper come from its workshops; the citadel has never fallen to assault.
ev.bochara.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.bochara.entry.title: Arriving at Bochara
ev.cabul.entry.body: Kabul — a fortress city in the eastern mountains, gateway to India. The Khyber caravans assemble here; lapis lazuli from Badakhshan and spices from Delhi change hands in the covered bazaar. The winter snows close the passes for four months; in summer the road to India is safe for a well-armed caravan.
ev.cabul.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.cabul.entry.title: Arriving at Cabul
ev.cacanfu.entry.body: Cacanfu is a noble city. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead; they have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts. For they have plenty of silk from which they weave stuffs of silk and gold, and sendals in large quantities. [There are also certain Christians at this place, who have a church.] And the city is at the head of an important territory containing numerous towns and villages.
ev.cacanfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cacanfu.entry.title: Concerning the Cities of Cacanfu and of Changlu
ev.cachanfu.entry.body: When you leave the castle, and travel about 20 miles westward, you come to a river called CARAMORAN, so big that no bridge can be thrown across it; for it is of immense width and depth, and reaches to the Great Ocean that encircles the Universe,—I mean the whole earth. On this river there are many cities and walled towns, and many merchants too therein, for much traffic takes place upon the river, there being a great deal of ginger and a great deal of silk produced in the country. Game birds here are in wonderful abundance, insomuch that you may buy at least three pheasants for a Venice groat of silver.
ev.cachanfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cachanfu.entry.title: Concerning the Great River Caramoran and the City of Cachanfu
ev.caffa.entry.body: Caffa, the Genoese colony on the Crimean shore, ringed by walls that the Tartars have never breached. From here, Tatar slaves, Russian furs, and Black Sea grain flow west to Constantinople and beyond. The harbor freezes in winter, but the trade never stops — sledges cross the ice to Tana when the ships cannot sail. The Genoese consul rules the city; his palace commands the harbor, and his galleys patrol the straits.
ev.caffa.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.caffa.entry.title: Arriving at Caffa
ev.caiju.entry.body: Caiju is a small city towards the south-east. The people are subject to the Great Kaan and have paper-money. It stands upon the river before mentioned. At this place are collected great quantities of corn and rice to be transported to the great city of Cambaluc for the use of the Kaan’s Court; for the grain for the Court all comes from this part of the country.
ev.caiju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.caiju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Caiju
ev.cail.entry.body: Cail is a great and noble city, and belongs to ASHAR, the eldest of the five brother Kings. It is at this city that all the ships touch that come from the west, as from Hormos and from Kis and from Aden, and all Arabia, laden with horses and with other things for sale. And this brings a great concourse of people from the country round about, and so there is great business done in this city of Cail. The King possesses vast treasures, and wears upon his person great store of rich jewels. He maintains great state and administers his kingdom with great equity, and extends great favour to merchants and foreigners, so that they are very glad to visit his city. This King has some 300 wives; for in those parts the man who has most wives is most thought of. As I told you before, there are in this great province of Maabar five crowned Kings, who are all own brothers born of one father and of one mother, and this king is one of them. Their mother is still living.
ev.cail.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.cail.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cail
ev.calatu.entry.body: Calatu is a great city, within a gulf which bears the name of the Gulf of Calatu. It is a noble city, and lies 600 miles from Dufar towards the north-west, upon the sea-shore. The people are Saracens, and are subject to Hormos. And whenever the Melic of Hormos is at war with some prince more potent than himself, he betakes himself to this city of Calatu, because it is very strong, both from its position and its fortifications. They grow no corn here, but get it from abroad; for every merchant-vessel that comes brings some. The haven is very large and good, and is frequented by numerous ships with goods from India, and from this city the spices and other merchandize are distributed among the cities and towns of the interior. They also export many good Arab horses from this to India. For, as I have told you before, the number of horses exported from this and the other cities to India yearly is something astonishing.
ev.calatu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.calatu.entry.title: Concerning the Gulf of Calatu and the City So Called
ev.camadi.entry.body: After you have ridden down hill those two days, you find yourself in a vast plain, and at the beginning thereof there is a city called CAMADI, which formerly was a great and noble place, but now is of little consequence, for the Tartars in their incursions have several times ravaged it. The plain whereof I speak is a very hot region; and the province that we now enter is called REOBARLES. The fruits of the country are dates, pistachioes, and apples of Paradise, with others of the like not found in our cold climate. [There are vast numbers of turtledoves, attracted by the abundance of fruits, but the Saracens never take them, for they hold them in abomination.] And on this plain there is a kind of bird called francolin, but different from the francolin of other countries, for their colour is a mixture of black and white, and the feet and beak are vermilion colour. The beasts also are peculiar; and first I will tell you of their oxen.
ev.camadi.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.camadi.entry.title: Of the City of Camadi and Its Ruins; Also Touching the Carauna Robbers
ev.cambaet.entry.body: Cambaet is a great kingdom lying further west. The people are Idolaters, and have a language of their own, and a king of their own, and are tributary to nobody. The North Star is here still more clearly visible; and henceforward the further you go west the higher you see it. There is a great deal of trade in this country. It produces indigo in great abundance; and they also make much fine buckram. There is also a quantity of cotton which is exported hence to many quarters; and there is a great trade in hides, which are very well dressed; with many other kinds of merchandize too tedious to mention.
ev.cambaet.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cambaet.entry.title: Concerning the Kingdom of Cambaet
ev.cambaluc.a.body: The palace of Cambaluc is the largest roofed building in the world. The great hall, where the Kaan holds his feasts and receives ambassadors, can hold six thousand men seated at table. The roof is painted vermilion, blue, green, and gold — dragons coil around the beams, and phoenixes spread their wings across the ceiling. The floors are of polished marble so clear that a man can see his reflection. The walls are hung with silk embroidered with scenes of hunts on horseback, battles between elephants and tigers, and the celestial palace where the gods feast. The Kaan sits on a raised dais at the northern end of the hall, on a throne of carved jade, so that his gaze falls on every guest.
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.admire: Stand before the great hall and marvel at its size
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.audience: Present yourself at the Kaan's court with gifts
ev.cambaluc.a.choice.talk_guards: Talk to the Kaan's guards about the empire
ev.cambaluc.a.title: The Palace of the Great Khan
ev.cambaluc.b.body: Each of Cambaluc's twelve gates opens onto a suburb larger than most cities of Christendom or Islam. In these suburbs, the merchants from every province of the Kaan's empire — Cathay, Manzi, Tangut, Tibet, the lands of the Golden Horde, Persia, and India — have their warehouses and counting-houses. A thousand cart-loads of silk enter the city every day. Forty cart-loads of pepper, spice, and precious goods are consumed daily. No poor person goes hungry in Cambaluc; the Kaan maintains public granaries that distribute rice and millet to anyone who asks. Outside every gate, there is a caravanserai for travelers who arrive after the curfew.
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.count: Count the cart-loads of silk entering the city in a day
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.granary: Visit the public granaries — no one goes hungry here
ev.cambaluc.b.choice.silk: Buy silk at the Cambaluc price
ev.cambaluc.b.title: The Twelve Suburbs
ev.cambaluc.c.body: In the great park behind the palace, the Kaan has caused a mountain to be raised — a hill of green jade, of jasper, and of lapis lazuli, brought block by block from the quarries of Badakhshan and Cotan. It is covered with evergreens: cedars, pines, and cypresses, each one dug up by the roots in distant forests, wrapped in silk and wet earth, and carried here on the backs of elephants. The trees do not know they have been moved; they grow as green as in their native soil. A thousand gardeners water them daily by hand, climbing the artificial mountain with buckets hung from shoulder-poles. The Kaan comes here in the evenings, when the shadows are long, and walks alone among the transplanted trees. No one may disturb him.
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.evening: Climb the hill at sunset and see the whole city
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.gardener: Talk to the gardeners who water the trees by hand
ev.cambaluc.c.choice.walk: Walk among the transplanted trees on the green hill
ev.cambaluc.c.title: The Mountain of Green Jade
ev.cambaluc.entry.body: You must know that the city of Cambaluc hath such a multitude of houses, and such a vast population inside the walls and outside, that it seems quite past all possibility. There is a suburb outside each of the gates, which are twelve in number; and these suburbs are so great that they contain more people than the city itself [for the suburb of one gate spreads in width till it meets the suburb of the next, whilst they extend in length some three or four miles]. In those suburbs lodge the foreign merchants and travellers, of whom there are always great numbers who have come to bring presents to the Emperor, or to sell articles at Court, or because the city affords so good a mart to attract traders. [There are in each of the suburbs, to a distance of a mile from the city, numerous fine hostelries for the lodgment of merchants from different parts of the world, and a special hostelry is assigned to each description of people, as if we should say there is one for the Lombards, another for the Germans, and a third for the Frenchmen.] And thus there are as many good houses outside of the city as inside, without counting those that belong to the great lords and barons, which are very numerous. You must know that it is forbidden to bury any dead body inside the city. If the body be that of an Idolater it is carried out beyond the city and suburbs to a remote place assigned for the purpose, to be burnt. And if it be of one belonging to a religion the custom of which is to bury, such as the Christian, the Saracen, or what not, it is also carried out beyond the suburbs to a distant place assigned for the purpose. And thus the city is preserved in a better and more healthy state. Moreover, no public woman resides inside the city, but all such abide outside in the suburbs. And ’tis wonderful what a vast number of these there are for the foreigners; it is a certain fact that there are more than 20,000 of them living by prostitution.
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the shìbó sī (市舶司)
ev.cambaluc.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.cambaluc.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cambaluc, and Its Great Traffic and Population
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.body: A chronologer of the Astronomical Bureau will sit with you fourteen days and teach the casting of hexagrams for the road. He does not ask after fortune. He asks after time and position — which season a road is open, and where a man stands when he chooses it.
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.ask: Hear how hexagrams speak of roads
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.choice.learn: Pay the fee and learn I Ching
ev.cambaluc.mentor_iching.title: I Ching at Khanbaliq
ev.campichu.entry.body: Campichu is also a city of Tangut, and a very great and noble one. Indeed it is the capital and place of government of the whole province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, Saracens, and Christians, and the latter have three very fine churches in the city, whilst the Idolaters have many minsters and abbeys after their fashion. In these they have an enormous number of idols, both small and great, certain of the latter being a good ten paces in stature; some of them being of wood, others of clay, and others yet of stone. They are all highly polished, and then covered with gold. The great idols of which I speak lie at length. And round about them there are other figures of considerable size, as if adoring and paying homage before them. Now, as I have not yet given you particulars about the customs of these Idolaters, I will proceed to tell you about them. You must know that there are among them certain religious recluses who lead a more virtuous life than the rest.
ev.campichu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.campichu.entry.title: Of the City of Campichu
ev.camul.entry.body: Hami — the first oasis east of the Great Desert, where the traveler who has survived the sand begins to breathe again. The people are Idolaters who once practiced a strange custom: they offered their wives to passing strangers as a mark of hospitality. The Great Khan forbade it, but the old people still speak of it. The melons of this district are the sweetest on the whole road.
ev.camul.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.camul.entry.title: Of the Province of Camul
ev.caracoron.entry.body: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there. And beside it there is a great citadel wherein is a fine palace in which the Governor resides.] ’Tis the first city that the Tartars possessed after they issued from their own country. And now I will tell you all about how they first acquired dominion and spread over the world. Originally the Tartars dwelt in the north on the borders of CHORCHA.
ev.caracoron.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.caracoron.entry.title: Of the City of Caracoron
ev.cascar.a.body: Cascar is the richest oasis on the Silk Road, where the melt-water from the Pamir and the Karakorum pours down the mountain valleys to feed a green paradise in the heart of the desert. Orchards of apricot, pomegranate, mulberry, walnut, and almond stretch for miles along the irrigation canals; the vines grow so heavy with grapes that the trellises must be replaced every year. The people are Muslims, but they keep many old customs from before the time of the Prophet. The grapes of Cascar are dried into raisins; the melons are the sweetest and largest in the world. A traveler who has crossed the mountains and tasted the melons of Cascar for the first time will speak of nothing else for a month.
ev.cascar.a.choice.grapes: Buy dried grapes from a vineyard on the mountain slope
ev.cascar.a.choice.melon: Buy a Cascar melon — the sweetest in the world
ev.cascar.a.choice.orchard: Walk the orchards watered by mountain snow
ev.cascar.a.title: The Garden of the Tarim
ev.cascar.b.body: The carpets of Cascar are woven so fine that a man can pass one through a finger-ring. The women of the city work for months on a single carpet, drawing the pattern from memory and knowing every dye by its smell: madder-root for red, indigo for blue, pomegranate rind for yellow, walnut hull for brown, and a secret mineral from the mountains for a green that fades only after a hundred years. The patterns are said to contain prayers — a carpet woven with the right designs will protect its owner from the evil eye, from snake-bite, and from the spirits of the desert. A merchant who buys a Cascar carpet never travels without it, and the carpets that reach the courts of Europe are treated as the treasure of kings.
ev.cascar.b.choice.carpet: Buy a carpet that can pass through a finger-ring
ev.cascar.b.choice.dyes: Buy the secret dye-stuffs from the dyers
ev.cascar.b.choice.learn_weave: Watch a weaver and learn the prayers in the patterns
ev.cascar.b.title: The Carpet Bazaar
ev.cascar.c.body: Outside the city walls, in the face of a limestone cliff, there is a cave where seven holy men are said to sleep. The Muslims say they have been sleeping since before the time of the Prophet, waiting for the Day of Judgment. The Christians say they are their own Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, miraculously transported here. A mosque and a chapel stand side by side at the cave entrance, sharing the same cliff-face wall. Pilgrims of both faiths come here, and neither side disturbs the other. The monks and the mullahs take turns sweeping the cave; the offerings of candles, incense, and silver coins are divided equally. It is said that anyone who stays in the cave overnight will hear the breathing of the sleepers.
ev.cascar.c.choice.both: Stay overnight in the cave and listen for their breathing
ev.cascar.c.choice.christian: Enter through the chapel and hear the Christian tale
ev.cascar.c.choice.muslim: Enter through the mosque and hear the Muslim tale
ev.cascar.c.title: The Shrine of the Seven Sleepers
ev.cascar.entry.body: Cascar is a region lying between north-east and east, and constituted a kingdom in former days, but now it is subject to the Great Kaan. The people worship Mahommet. There are a good number of towns and villages, but the greatest and finest is Cascar itself. The inhabitants live by trade and handicrafts; they have beautiful gardens and vineyards, and fine estates, and grow a great deal of cotton. From this country many merchants go forth about the world on trading journeys. The natives are a wretched, niggardly set of people; they eat and drink in miserable fashion. There are in the country many Nestorian Christians, who have churches of their own. The people of the country have a peculiar language, and the territory extends for five days’ journey.
ev.cascar.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the bājgāh (toll-house)
ev.cascar.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.cascar.entry.title: Of the Kingdom of Cascar
ev.chamba.entry.body: You must know that on leaving the port of Zayton you sail west-south-west for 1500 miles, and then you come to a country called CHAMBA, a very rich region, having a king of its own. The people are Idolaters and pay a yearly tribute to the Great Kaan, which consists of elephants and nothing but elephants. And I will tell you how they came to pay this tribute. It happened in the year of Christ 1278 that the Great Kaan sent a Baron of his called Sagatu with a great force of horse and foot against this King of Chamba, and this Baron opened the war on a great scale against the King and his country. Now the King was a very aged man, nor had he such a force as the Baron had. And when he saw what havoc the Baron was making with his kingdom he was grieved to the heart. So he bade messengers get ready and despatched them to the Great Kaan.
ev.chamba.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.chamba.entry.title: Of the Great Country Called Chamba
ev.chandu.a.body: The Great Kaan has a summer palace at Chandu built entirely of gilded cane — the columns, the walls, the roof-beams, everything. The cane is harvested from a forest in the south of Manzi, split, lacquered, and gilded with gold leaf before being lashed together with silken cords. The palace can be taken down and moved when the Kaan travels, for it is held together only by the silk bindings. Dragons in green, blue, vermilion, and gold coil up every pillar. Inside, the floors are laid with marble slabs so polished that they reflect the gilded ceiling. No other building in the world is so light and yet so splendid.
ev.chandu.a.choice.admire: Admire the palace from the meadow outside
ev.chandu.a.choice.enter: Bribe the guards and step inside the gilded cane palace
ev.chandu.a.choice.sketch: Spend a day sketching the palace in detail
ev.chandu.a.title: The Cane Palace
ev.chandu.b.body: Behind the palace, enclosed by a wall that runs for sixteen miles, is the Kaan's game park — a forest so dense and so large that a man on horseback cannot cross it in a single day. It is stocked with deer, boar, wild ass, bear, and leopard for the Kaan's sport. At the center is a lake fed by a stream, and on the lake every species of waterfowl known to man. The Kaan rides here with his falconers, his huntsmen, and his cheetah-keepers. In one corner of the park, a herd of a thousand white mares is kept — their milk is reserved for the imperial family alone, and the mares are so sacred that no one of lower rank may ride them, touch them, or even walk in their pasture.
ev.chandu.b.choice.falcon: Hire a falconer and hunt with the Kaan's own birds
ev.chandu.b.choice.horses: Find a gap in the wall and watch the sacred white mares
ev.chandu.b.choice.walk: Walk the edge of the sixteen-mile wall
ev.chandu.b.title: The Game Park
ev.chandu.c.body: In a meadow at the northern end of the park, the monks of the Palace of the Spring tend the sacred white mares. These animals are not ridden or worked. They are milked twice a day, and the milk is carried in golden vessels to the Kaan's table. No one of lesser rank may taste it. Once a year, on the day of the great Mongol festival, the Kaan himself rides to the meadow and pours the milk on the ground as an offering to the spirits of the Eternal Blue Sky and the Golden Earth — a rite that goes back to the days when the Mongols were a tribe of wandering herdsmen on the northern steppe, long before they ruled the world. No foreigner has ever been permitted to witness this ceremony.
ev.chandu.c.choice.listen: Ask a monk what the ceremony means
ev.chandu.c.choice.offering: Pour an offering to the Eternal Blue Sky
ev.chandu.c.choice.watch_mares: Watch the monks milk the white mares at dawn
ev.chandu.c.title: The Meadow of the Milky Kine
ev.chandu.entry.body: And when you have ridden three days from the city last mentioned, between north-east and north, you come to a city called CHANDU, which was built by the Kaan now reigning. There is at this place a very fine marble Palace, the rooms of which are all gilt and painted with figures of men and beasts and birds, and with a variety of trees and flowers, all executed with such exquisite art that you regard them with delight and astonishment. Round this Palace a wall is built, inclosing a compass of 16 miles, and inside the Park there are fountains and rivers and brooks, and beautiful meadows, with all kinds of wild animals (excluding such as are of ferocious nature), which the Emperor has procured and placed there to supply food for his gerfalcons and hawks, which he keeps there in mew. Of these there are more than 200 gerfalcons alone, without reckoning the other hawks. The Kaan himself goes every week to see his birds sitting in mew, and sometimes he rides through the park with a leopard behind him on his horse’s croup; and then if he sees any animal that takes his fancy, he slips his leopard at it, and the game when taken is made over to feed the hawks in mew. This he does for diversion. Moreover [at a spot in the Park where there is a charming wood] he has another Palace built of cane, of which I must give you a description. It is gilt all over, and most elaborately finished inside. [It is stayed on gilt and lackered columns, on each of which is a dragon all gilt, the tail of which is attached to the column whilst the head supports the architrave, and the claws likewise are stretched out right and left to support the architrave.] The roof, like the rest, is formed of canes, covered with a varnish so strong and excellent that no amount of rain will rot them. These canes are a good 3 palms in girth, and from 10 to 15 paces in length.
ev.chandu.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods to the darughachi (overseer)
ev.chandu.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.chandu.entry.title: Of the City of Chandu, and the Kaan’s Palace There
ev.charchan.entry.body: Charchan is a Province of Great Turkey, lying between north-east and east. The people worship Mahommet. There are numerous towns and villages, and the chief city of the kingdom bears its name, Charchan. The Province contains rivers which bring down Jasper and Chalcedony, and these are carried for sale into Cathay, where they fetch great prices. The whole of the Province is sandy, and so is the road all the way from Pein, and much of the water that you find is bitter and bad. However, at some places you do find fresh and sweet water.
ev.charchan.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.charchan.entry.title: Of the Province of Charchan
ev.chinangli.entry.body: Chinangli is a city of Cathay as you go south, and it belongs to the Great Kaan; the people are Idolaters, and have paper-money. There runs through the city a great and wide river, on which a large traffic in silk goods and spices and other costly merchandize passes up and down. When you travel south from Chinangli for five days, you meet everywhere with fine towns and villages, the people of which are all Idolaters, and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by trade and handicrafts, and have all the necessaries of life in great abundance. But there is nothing particular to mention on the way till you come, at the end of those five days, to TADINFU. This, you must know, is a very great city, and in old times was the seat of a great kingdom; but the Great Kaan conquered it by force of arms. Nevertheless it is still the noblest city in all those provinces. There are very great merchants here, who trade on a great scale, and the abundance of silk is something marvellous.
ev.chinangli.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.chinangli.entry.title: Arriving at CHINANGLI
ev.chinghianfu.entry.body: Chinghianfu is a city of Manzi. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan, and have paper-money, and live by handicrafts and trade. They have plenty of silk, from which they make sundry kinds of stuffs of silk and gold. There are great and wealthy merchants in the place; plenty of game is to be had, and of all kinds of victual. There are in this city two churches of Nestorian Christians which were established in the year of our Lord 1278; and I will tell you how that happened.
ev.chinghianfu.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.chinghianfu.entry.title: Of the City of Chinghianfu
ev.chinginju.entry.body: Leaving the city of Chinghianfu and travelling three days south-east through a constant succession of busy and thriving towns and villages, you arrive at the great and noble city of CHINGINJU. The people are Idolaters, use paper-money, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They live by trade and handicrafts, and they have plenty of silk. They have also abundance of game, and of all manner of victuals, for it is a most productive territory. Now I must tell you of an evil deed that was done, once upon a time, by the people of this city, and how dearly they paid for it.
ev.chinginju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.chinginju.entry.title: Of the City of Chinginju and the Slaughter of Certain Alans There
ev.cobinan.entry.body: Cobinan is a large town. The people worship Mahommet. There is much Iron and Steel and _Ondanique_, and they make steel mirrors of great size and beauty. They also prepare both _Tutia_ (a thing very good for the eyes) and _Spodium_; and I will tell you the process. They have a vein of a certain earth which has the required quality, and this they put into a great flaming furnace, whilst over the furnace there is an iron grating. The smoke and moisture, expelled from the earth of which I speak, adhere to the iron grating, and thus form _Tutia_, whilst the slag that is left after burning is the _Spodium_.
ev.cobinan.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.cobinan.entry.title: Concerning the City of Cobinan and the Things That Are Made There
ev.coigangiu.entry.body: Huaiyin — a boat-town on the Grand Canal. Every family keeps a sampan; the children learn to row before they learn to walk. The grain fleet passes through here in autumn on its way to Cambaluc; the inns are full of boatmen, and the smell of river-fish frying drifts across the water from dawn till midnight.
ev.coigangiu.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.coigangiu.entry.title: Arriving at Coigangiu
ev.coiganju.entry.body: Coiganju is, as I have told you already, a very large city standing at the entrance to Manzi. The people are Idolaters and burn their dead, and are subject to the Great Kaan. They have a vast amount of shipping, as I mentioned before in speaking of the River Caramoran. And an immense quantity of merchandize comes hither, for the city is the seat of government for this part of the country. Owing to its being on the river, many cities send their produce thither to be again thence distributed in every direction.
ev.coiganju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.coiganju.entry.title: Concerning the City of Coiganju
ev.coilum.entry.body: When you quit Maabar and go 500 miles towards the south-west you come to the kingdom of COILUM. The people are Idolaters, but there are also some Christians and some Jews. The natives have a language of their own, and a King of their own, and are tributary to no one. A great deal of brazil is got here which is called _brazil Coilumin_ from the country which produces it; ’tis of very fine quality. Good ginger also grows here, and it is known by the same name of _Coilumin_ after the country. Pepper too grows in great abundance throughout this country, and I will tell you how.
ev.coilum.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.coilum.entry.title: Of the Kingdom of Coilum
ev.constantinopolis.entry.body: Constantinople, the Queen of Cities. The dome of Hagia Sophia still rises above the Golden Horn, but the Latin emperors have stripped her of treasure. Venetian and Genoese merchants own the best quarters; the Greek merchants watch from Galata with envy.
ev.constantinopolis.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.constantinopolis.entry.title: Arriving at Constantinopolis
ev.cotan.a.body: From the mountains above Cotan, two rivers carry down stones of jade — the white jade that is like congealed mutton-fat, and the green jade that is like the first leaves of spring after a long desert winter. The men of Cotan wade into the cold water in autumn, when the rivers run low, and feel for the stones with their bare feet. When they find one, they dive and bring it up. The largest stones are sold to the Kaan's agents, who send them to Cambaluc to be carved into cups, bracelets, and belt-buckles for the court. A fine piece of mutton-fat jade is worth more than its weight in gold. All the jade that reaches the Great Kaan's court in Cambaluc — and all that reaches Persia, India, and the West — comes from these two rivers.
ev.cotan.a.choice.jade: Buy a piece of mutton-fat jade — worth its weight in gold
ev.cotan.a.choice.wade: Wade into the cold river and feel for jade with your feet
ev.cotan.a.choice.watch: Watch the divers from the bank and learn their craft
ev.cotan.a.title: The Jade Rivers
ev.cotan.b.body: The country around Cotan is planted with mulberry trees as far as the eye can see. The women of the city spin silk finer than any in Cathay — a single thread, finer than a human hair, can run for a thousand paces without breaking. The silk is dyed with saffron for yellow, indigo for blue, madder for red, and cochineal for crimson. The looms are worked by two women sitting opposite each other; they pass the shuttle back and forth while singing a song that keeps the rhythm. A bolt of Cotan silk large enough to make a robe sells for its weight in silver in the bazaars of Cambaluc. The Kaan's tax-collectors demand silk as tribute, and the weavers pay it willingly, for the Kaan's agents pay more than any merchant.
ev.cotan.b.choice.dyes: Buy dye samples — saffron, indigo, madder, cochineal
ev.cotan.b.choice.silk: Buy a bolt of Cotan silk — finer than human hair
ev.cotan.b.choice.weave: Sit with the women at the looms and learn their song
ev.cotan.b.title: The Silk Looms of Cotan
ev.cotan.c.body: Beyond the living city, on the old river terrace where the water no longer flows, the sand has buried an older Cotan — a city of a thousand monasteries, a hundred stupas, and more painted caves than any man could visit in a lifetime. The wind uncovers fragments day by day: a painted face of a bodhisattva with kohl-rimmed eyes, a hand raised in blessing, lotus petals in gold and vermilion, halo-fires of indigo blue. The old people say the dust of these walls is holy — they mix it with water and drink it as medicine. The archaeologists of the court in Cambaluc send expeditions to catalogue the ruins, but the desert reclaims whatever they uncover within a season. The Buddha Dust blows east on the wind that crosses the Taklamakan.
ev.cotan.c.choice.explore: Dig in the buried city of a thousand monasteries
ev.cotan.c.choice.fragment: Collect a painted fragment — a bodhisattva's hand
ev.cotan.c.choice.listen_elder: Ask an elder why the people drink the dust as medicine
ev.cotan.c.title: The Buddha Dust
ev.cotan.entry.body: Cotan is a province lying between north-east and east, and is eight days’ journey in length. The people are subject to the Great Kaan, and are all worshippers of Mahommet. There are numerous towns and villages in the country, but Cotan, the capital, is the most noble of all, and gives its name to the kingdom. Everything is to be had there in plenty, including abundance of cotton, [with flax, hemp, wheat, wine, and the like]. The people have vineyards and gardens and estates. They live by commerce and manufactures, and are no soldiers.
ev.cotan.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the bājgāh (toll-house)
ev.cotan.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.cotan.entry.title: Of a Province Called Cotan
ev.ctesiphon.entry.body: Ctesiphon — the ghost of Sassanian glory. The great arch of the Taq-i-Kisra still stands, the largest brick span in the world, but the palace halls are empty now, and the Tigris has shifted its course away from the ruins.
ev.ctesiphon.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.ctesiphon.entry.title: Arriving at Ctesiphon
ev.damascus.entry.body: Damascus — the garden city of the Umayyads, where canals fed by the Barada River water orchards of apricot and almond within the walls. Its steel blades — watered with a pattern like running water — are the finest in the world. Its brocades of gold and silk clothe sultans from Cairo to Delhi. The Great Mosque, once a church, once a temple, now rises above the old city; the minaret of the Bride is visible from three days' journey away.
ev.damascus.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.damascus.entry.title: Arriving at Damascus
ev.delli.entry.body: Delhi — the capital of the Sultanate, a city of mosques, minarets, and markets that swallows caravans from Khorasan and Bengal alike. The Sultan's cavalry — ten thousand Turkic horsemen — patrols the walls. The bazaars sell horses from Arabia, swords from Damascus, and slaves from Africa. No city in India is richer or more dangerous.
ev.delli.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.delli.entry.title: Arriving at Delli
ev.dongola.entry.body: Dongola — a Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile, Christian since the sixth century. The cathedral of painted saints overlooks the river; the king still mints coins with the cross. Caravans bring gold and ivory from the interior and slaves from the pagan south. The desert on either side is waterless for ten days' journey.
ev.dongola.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.dongola.entry.title: Arriving at Dongola
ev.dufar.entry.body: Dufar is a great and noble and fine city, and lies 500 miles to the north-west of Esher. The people are Saracens, and have a Count for their chief, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden; for this city still belongs to the Province of Aden. It stands upon the sea and has a very good haven, so that there is a great traffic of shipping between this and India; and the merchants take hence great numbers of Arab horses to that market, making great profits thereby. This city has under it many other towns and villages. Much white incense is produced here, and I will tell you how it grows.
ev.dufar.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.dufar.entry.title: Concerning the City of Dufar
ev.edessa.entry.body: Edessa — an ancient Christian city on the edge of the Turcoman steppe, once home to the fabled Mandylion, the cloth that bore Christ's face. Now a frontier fortress, its walls scarred by siege and counter-siege. The caravans from Mosul water their camels here before crossing into Anatolia; the trade in horses, carpets, and cotton keeps the bazaar alive.
ev.edessa.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.edessa.entry.title: Arriving at Edessa
ev.egrigaia.entry.body: Starting again from Erguiul you ride eastward for eight days, and then come to a province called EGRIGAIA, containing numerous cities and villages, and belonging to Tangut. The capital city is called CALACHAN. The people are chiefly Idolaters, but there are fine churches belonging to the Nestorian Christians. They are all subjects of the Great Kaan. They make in this city great quantities of camlets of camel’s wool, the finest in the world; and some of the camlets that they make are white, for they have white camels, and these are the best of all. Merchants purchase these stuffs here, and carry them over the world for sale.
ev.egrigaia.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.egrigaia.entry.title: Of the Kingdom of Egrigaia
ev.ephesus.entry.body: Ephesus — the harbor that silted up. The great Temple of Artemis is a memory; the Apostle John's basilica draws a trickle of pilgrims. Silk from the inland valleys still reaches the remaining wharves, bound for Smyrna and the sea.
ev.ephesus.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.ephesus.entry.title: Arriving at Ephesus
ev.esher.entry.body: Esher is a great city lying in a north-westerly direction from the last, and 400 miles distant from the Port of Aden. It has a king, who is subject to the Soldan of Aden. He has a number of towns and villages under him, and administers his territory well and justly. The people are Saracens. The place has a very good haven, wherefore many ships from India come thither with various cargoes; and they export many good chargers thence to India. A great deal of white incense grows in this country, and brings in a great revenue to the Prince; for no one dares sell it to any one else; and whilst he takes it from the people at 10 livres of gold for the hundredweight, he sells it to the merchants at 60 livres, so his profit is immense. Dates also grow very abundantly here. The people have no corn but rice, and very little of that; but plenty is brought from abroad, for it sells here at a good profit.
ev.esher.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzā without delay
ev.esher.entry.title: Concerning the City of Esher
ev.etzina.entry.body: When you leave the city of Campichu you ride for twelve days, and then reach a city called ETZINA, which is towards the north on the verge of the Sandy Desert; it belongs to the Province of Tangut. The people are Idolaters, and possess plenty of camels and cattle, and the country produces a number of good falcons, both Sakers and Lanners. The inhabitants live by their cultivation and their cattle, for they have no trade.
ev.etzina.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.etzina.entry.title: Of the City of Etzina
ev.fuju.entry.body: Now this city of Fuju is the key of the kingdom which is called CHONKA, and which is one of the nine great divisions of Manzi. The city is a seat of great trade and great manufactures. The people are Idolaters and subject to the Great Kaan. And a large garrison is maintained there by that prince to keep the kingdom in peace and subjection. For the city is one which is apt to revolt on very slight provocation. There flows through the middle of this city a great river, which is about a mile in width, and many ships are built at the city which are launched upon this river.
ev.fuju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.fuju.entry.title: Concerning the Greatness of the City of Fuju
ev.hierusalem.entry.body: Jerusalem — the city that three faiths call holy. The Dome of the Rock glitters above the Western Wall; the Holy Sepulchre echoes with Latin, Greek, Armenian, and Coptic chant. Pilgrims pay a tax at the gate; the Mamluk guard watches from the Citadel.
ev.hierusalem.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.hierusalem.entry.title: Arriving at Hierusalem
ev.ispahan.entry.body: Isfahan — the garden city of the Persian plateau, where the Friday Mosque with its twin domes of turquoise tile has stood since the days of the Seljuk sultans. The Zayandeh River waters a hundred gardens within the walls. Its workshops produce the finest miniature paintings, the deepest blue tiles, and the softest carpets in the Ilkhan's lands. The covered bridge of the Jews crosses the river; merchants from India, Khorasan, and Anatolia crowd its arcades.
ev.ispahan.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.ispahan.entry.title: Arriving at Ispahan
ev.java-major.entry.body: Java the Great — an island kingdom of immense wealth, where pepper, nutmeg, and cloves grow in the volcanic soil. The Shahbandar of the port taxes every ship that enters; no man has ever sailed around the island, which the natives claim extends southward without end. The king pays no tribute to any power; his war-elephants and his fleet of a thousand prahus are the terror of the surrounding seas.
ev.java-major.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.java-major.entry.title: Arriving at Java Major
ev.kenjanfu.entry.body: And when you leave the city of Cachanfu of which I have spoken, and travel eight days westward, you meet with cities and boroughs abounding in trade and industry, and quantities of beautiful trees, and gardens, and fine plains planted with mulberries, which are the trees on the leaves of which the silkworms do feed. The people are all Idolaters. There is also plenty of game of all sorts, both of beasts and birds. And when you have travelled those eight days’ journey, you come to that great city which I mentioned, called KENJANFU. A very great and fine city it is, and the capital of the kingdom of Kenjanfu, which in old times was a noble, rich, and powerful realm, and had many great and wealthy and puissant kings. But now the king thereof is a prince called MANGALAI, the son of the Great Kaan, who hath given him this realm, and crowned him king thereof. It is a city of great trade and industry.
ev.kenjanfu.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the gate without delay
ev.kenjanfu.entry.title: Concerning the City of Kenjanfu
ev.kerman.entry.body: Kerman is a kingdom which is also properly in Persia, and formerly it had a hereditary prince. Since the Tartars conquered the country the rule is no longer hereditary, but the Tartar sends to administer whatever lord he pleases. In this kingdom are produced the stones called turquoises in great abundance; they are found in the mountains, where they are extracted from the rocks. There are also plenty of veins of steel and _Ondanique_. The people are very skilful in making harness of war; their saddles, bridles, spurs, swords, bows, quivers, and arms of every kind, are very well made indeed according to the fashion of those parts. The ladies of the country and their daughters also produce exquisite needlework in the embroidery of silk stuffs in different colours, with figures of beasts and birds, trees and flowers, and a variety of other patterns. They work hangings for the use of noblemen so deftly that they are marvels to see, as well as cushions, pillows quilts, and all sorts of things. In the mountains of Kerman are found the best falcons in the world.
ev.kerman.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.kerman.entry.title: Concerning the Kingdom of Kerman
ev.keshimur.entry.body: Keshimur also is a Province inhabited by a people who are Idolaters and have a language of their own. They have an astonishing acquaintance with the devilries of enchantment; insomuch that they make their idols to speak. They can also by their sorceries bring on changes of weather and produce darkness, and do a number of things so extraordinary that no one without seeing them would believe them. Indeed, this country is the very original source from which Idolatry has spread abroad. In this direction you can proceed further till you come to the Sea of India. The men are brown and lean, but the women, taking them as brunettes, are very beautiful. The food of the people is flesh, and milk, and rice. The clime is finely tempered, being neither very hot nor very cold. There are numbers of towns and villages in the country, but also forests and desert tracts, and strong passes, so that the people have no fear of anybody, and keep their independence, with a king of their own to rule and do justice.
ev.keshimur.entry.choice.pass: Pass through the darvāzeh without delay
ev.keshimur.entry.title: Of the Province of Keshimur
ev.kinsay.a.body: Kinsay is a city built on water — it is said there are twelve thousand bridges of stone, and all of them are so tall that a ship with its mast raised can pass beneath without lowering the yard. Some have shops built on them. The streets are canals; the boats are the carriages. A man could spend his whole life in Kinsay and never walk more than a hundred paces on dry land. From the top of the drum-tower in the center of the city, a hundred canals radiate in every direction, each one lined with stone embankments as straight as a sword-cut. The city has no walls — the water is its wall, and the Kaan maintains a fleet of patrol boats to keep the peace.
ev.kinsay.a.choice.boat: Hire a boat and spend the day on the canals
ev.kinsay.a.choice.tower: Climb the drum-tower and see the hundred canals below
ev.kinsay.a.choice.walk: Walk the bridges and see if you can count them all
ev.kinsay.a.title: The Twelve Thousand Bridges
ev.kinsay.b.body: The markets of Kinsay are ten great squares, each one half a mile on a side, surrounded by double-storied warehouses with shops below and counting-houses above. Every fish of the sea and lake, every fruit of the earth, every fabric known to man, every spice and drug and perfume is sold in one of these ten squares. Forty cart-loads of pepper pass through the customs house every day. The main street that connects the markets is paved with stone and brick so finely joined that no water stands on it even in the heaviest rain. On either side are bathhouses and restaurants where a man can bathe in hot water perfumed with flowers and then dine on ten courses for a few copper coins.
ev.kinsay.b.choice.bath: Bathe in perfumed water and dine on ten courses
ev.kinsay.b.choice.count_pepper: Count the forty cart-loads of pepper passing the customs
ev.kinsay.b.choice.pepper: Buy two sacks of pepper from the customs house
ev.kinsay.b.title: The Ten Great Markets
ev.kinsay.c.body: On the West Lake, just outside the city walls, the pleasure boats of Kinsay float day and night — painted in gold, blue, and vermilion, with silk awnings and cushioned seats. Each boat is a floating pavilion. Musicians play the pipa and the guqin on the open deck. Dancers perform in costumes embroidered with phoenixes. Wine flows from porcelain cups, and lanterns hang from the awning poles, their reflections dancing on the black water. The lake is so large that a circuit takes a whole day. The islands in the lake have pleasure-palaces where the wealthy hold banquets that last three days. A man who has not seen the West Lake by moonlight has not seen the most beautiful thing in the empire of the Kaan.
ev.kinsay.c.choice.boat: Hire a pleasure boat with musicians and wine
ev.kinsay.c.choice.moonlight: Wait for moonlight — the most beautiful thing in the empire
ev.kinsay.c.choice.watch: Stand on the shore and watch the floating palaces
ev.kinsay.c.title: The Pleasure Boats of the West Lake
ev.kinsay.entry.body: When you have left the city of Changan and have travelled for three days through a splendid country, passing a number of towns and villages, you arrive at the most noble city of KINSAY, a name which is as much as to say in our tongue “The City of Heaven,” as I told you before. And since we have got thither I will enter into particulars about its magnificence; and these are well worth the telling, for the city is beyond dispute the finest and the noblest in the world. In this we shall speak according to the written statement which the Queen of this Realm sent to Bayan the conqueror of the country for transmission to the Great Kaan, in order that he might be aware of the surpassing grandeur of the city and might be moved to save it from destruction or injury. I will tell you all the truth as it was set down in that document. For truth it was, as the said Messer Marco Polo at a later date was able to witness with his own eyes. And now we shall rehearse those particulars. First and foremost, then, the document stated the city of Kinsay to be so great that it hath an hundred miles of compass. And there are in it twelve thousand bridges of stone, for the most part so lofty that a great fleet could pass beneath them. And let no man marvel that there are so many bridges, for you see the whole city stands as it were in the water and surrounded by water, so that a great many bridges are required to give free passage about it. [And though the bridges be so high the approaches are so well contrived that carts and horses do cross them.] The document aforesaid also went on to state that there were in this city twelve guilds of the different crafts, and that each guild had 12,000 houses in the occupation of its workmen. Each of these houses contains at least 12 men, whilst some contain 20 and some 40,—not that these are all masters, but inclusive of the journeymen who work under the masters.
ev.kinsay.entry.choice.customs: Declare your goods at the shìbó sī (市舶司)
ev.kinsay.entry.choice.lore: Ask what men say of this city
ev.kinsay.entry.title: Arriving at GREAT CITY OF KINSAY
ev.kiovia.entry.body: Kiev — the mother of Russian cities, now a tributary of the Golden Horde. Its golden domes still shine above the Dnieper, though the Mongol sack of a generation ago is still visible in the ruined quarters. The Tatar baskak collects the taxes; the river trade has slowed, but furs, wax, and honey still find their way south to the Black Sea ports.
ev.kiovia.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.kiovia.entry.title: Arriving at Kiovia
ev.linju.entry.body: On leaving the city of Sinju-matu you travel for eight days towards the south, always coming to great and rich towns and villages flourishing with trade and manufactures. The people are all subjects of the Great Kaan, use paper-money, and burn their dead. At the end of those eight days you come to the city of LINJU, in the province of the same name of which it is the capital. It is a rich and noble city, and the men are good soldiers, natheless they carry on great trade and manufactures. There is great abundance of game in both beasts and birds, and all the necessaries of life are in profusion.
ev.linju.entry.choice.look: Rest and ask what men say of this place
ev.linju.entry.title: Concerning the Cities of Linju and Piju
ev.lop.bazaar.body: The bazaar of Lop spills out of the town walls onto the gravel plain where the caravans assemble. Merchants from Khotan and Sachiu spread their goods on carpets laid on the ground: bolts of silk, sacks of dried melon, blocks of pressed tea, and — rarest of all — river jade from the streams above Cotan. The jade merchants sit apart, their stones displayed on black velvet to show the color. A piece of mutton-fat white jade the size of a man's fist costs more than a camel. The trader smiles and holds it up to the sun; the light passes through it like water.
ev.lop.bazaar.choice.ask_prices: Ask where the jade comes from
ev.lop.bazaar.title: The Jade Market
ev.lop.caravanserai.body: The caravanserai of Lop is the last way-station before the Great Desert — a vast courtyard surrounded by stables and sleeping-platforms, filled with the smell of camel, dust, and cooking-fires. Travelers who have just crossed the desert sit stunned in the shade, drinking water mixed with a little salt to restore what the sand has taken. Those about to cross listen to their stories with mounting dread. The innkeeper offers guides, provisions, and advice, taking payment in silver and giving change in dried meat. The walls are covered with graffiti in a dozen scripts: names of travelers who made it, and prayers for those who did not.
ev.lop.caravanserai.choice.wait_caravan: Wait for a caravan (8 days, 120 coins)
ev.lop.caravanserai.title: The Caravanserai
ev.lop.entry.body: Lop is a large town at the edge of the Desert of Lop, and travellers who mean to cross rest here a week to refresh themselves and their beasts. Then they load provision for a month for man and beast, and go forward. You must know that the desert is said to be so long that no one could ride across it in a year; and where it is narrowest it still takes a month. It is all sand and barren mountains, with nothing at all to eat, but in a day and a night you find sweet water, enough for fifty or a hundred persons with their beasts.
ev.lop.entry.choice.ask: Ask what men say of the desert crossing
ev.lop.entry.choice.rest: Rest half a day by the road
ev.lop.entry.title: The Town of Lop
ev.lop.shrine.body: In the low cliffs east of the town, the wind has carved a labyrinth of shallow caves. The walls are covered with charcoal drawings left by travelers over centuries: camels, horsemen, prayers in Arabic and Sanskrit, names and dates. A small Buddhist shrine occupies the largest cave — a clay Buddha painted with cheap gold leaf, surrounded by burnt-out incense sticks and offerings of dried fruit. The monks are gone, but the shrine-keeper, an old Tangut woman with a leathery face, tends the lamps and accepts whatever coins the travelers leave.
ev.lop.shrine.title: The Caves of Lop
